It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.
Optimization and Control.comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics

Optimization and Control.title: Risk-Aware Unit Commitment in District Heating Networks: Chance-Constrained and CVaR Optimization Under Demand Uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: While district heating networks are a key component of the energy transition, their operational planning is challenging due to substantial uncertainty in heat demand. We study how unit-commitment schedules can account for this uncertainty and what reliability costs. By adapting chance-constrained programming (CC) and conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) optimization to the mixed-integer unit-commitment problem for district-heating networks, we can compute optimal unit-commitment schedules under demand uncertainty. We generate heat demand scenarios using a Bayesian model, which explicitly quantifies forecasting uncertainty and yields predictive distributions as input to the network optimization. To handle the inherent uncertainty in heat demand, we apply two stochastic optimization approaches that exploit this distribution: chance-constrained programming limits the probability of unmet demand, and in our scenario-based setting reduces to a deterministic MIP in which demand is replaced by an empirical quantile, while CVaR optimization penalizes severe shortfalls in the tail of the distribution. We evaluate the approaches both on real-world data from the Berlin district heating network and on a benchmark set of synthetic, realistically parameterized instances of varying sizes. The results show that the two methods are complementary: CC cheaply traces the high-reliability end of the cost--reliability trade-off and reveals the physical reliability limit of the network, whereas CVaR covers the low-cost, risk-tolerant regime at considerably higher computational effort.

Optimization and Control.title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.

Optimization and Control.title: Douglas-Rachford splitting method for nonconvex stochastic optimal control
Optimization and Control.summary: Motivated by the numerical resolution of stochastic optimal control problems, particularly those involving nonlinear dynamics, we investigate the convergence properties of the Douglas-Rachford splitting algorithm in a nonconvex and infinite-dimensional setting. We introduce an extension of the method that applies when one component of the objective function is continuously differentiable with a locally Lipschitz gradient, while the other is weakly lower semicontinuous with a bounded domain.

Optimization and Control.title: Effective Dual Subgradient Methods Through Sequential Subgradient-Aligned Rays
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we propose an efficient subgradient-based framework, referred to as the sequential subgradient-aligned rays (SSAR) method, for improving the convergence performance of the dual subgradient method. In particular, the proposed method identifies and exploits a finite sequence of rays, when available, as the dual subgradient method evolves, along each of which a subgradient of the negative dual function remains constant and aligns with the ray. While the dual variable iterates remain on each identified ray, a constant stepsize associated with the ray is employed, with the associated constant stepsizes decreasing from one ray to the next. This approach yields constant decrements in the negative dual function values while the dual variable iterates remain on the associated rays, enabling the dual variable iterates to progress more quickly toward a dual optimal solution. We then show that the proposed SSAR method can be leveraged to improve the performance of the dual decomposition method for minimizing the average of local loss functions associated with multiple agents that share a common decision variable, a widely used problem formulation in many large-scale real-world applications. In particular, the SSAR method improves the convergence performance of the corresponding dual decomposition method while also reducing its communication cost. Numerical experiments on a least squares regression problem and a logistic regression problem using real datasets are conducted to evaluate the performance of the SSAR method.
Optimization and Control.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Optimization and Control.title: Online Feedback Optimization for Constrained Stochastic Problems with Decision-Dependent Distributions
Optimization and Control.summary: Online feedback optimization (OFO) leverages real-time output measurements to optimize the operation of networked systems without requiring full knowledge of system dynamics or disturbances. We develop an OFO approach for constrained stochastic optimization problems in which the distribution of the system's random parameters shifts in response to the control actions. We propose a projected primal-dual algorithm where the true dual constraint sets are replaced by surrogate sets. Our main result is an upper bound on the mean-square tracking error, which decomposes into four interpretable terms reflecting: (i) the stochasticity of the problem, (ii) output measurement errors, (iii) time-variability of the problem, and (iv) the mismatch between surrogate and true dual constraint sets. The theory is illustrated in a numerical experiment for power grids with price-responsive assets.
Optimization and Control.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure. This manuscript is an extended version of an article accepted for publication in IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS)

Optimization and Control.title: A Resource Allocation Tournament
Optimization and Control.summary: We introduce and analyze a round-robin simultaneous resource allocation contest, motivated by sports leagues and other competitive environments where agents must distribute limited resources across multiple encounters. Players allocate resources in advance to matches against all opponents, and match outcomes are determined by relative allocations. We study two payoff schemes: total points, where players accumulate rewards for each win, and winner-takes-all, where only the tournament winner is rewarded. For three players, we provide complete equilibrium characterizations under both schemes. For four or more players, we show that the total points payoff admits Blotto-type equilibria, while the winner-takes-all payoff requires numerical and algorithmic analysis. To address this, we develop a best-response dynamics algorithm with stochastic inertia and use it to approximate equilibria in games with four and five players.

Optimization and Control.title: Benign cubic and quartic forms on the sphere
Optimization and Control.summary: One considers the NP-hard problem of minimizing real cubic and quartic forms on the Euclidean unit sphere. One first extends the Hessian spectral characterization of local minima by the author. In particular one provides a gap-depth characterization of negative global and spurious minima, and proves that the minimum value of an odd degree-d form is recovered (up to the factor d(d -1)) by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of its ambient Hessian over the sphere (and equivalently the unit ball). Next, one exhibits several classes of benign families of cubic and quartic forms (i.e. with no spurious local minima on the sphere) and prove that some are robust to small coefficient perturbation (i.e. the resulting form remains benign even if it leaves the initial family). Therefore the class of benign cubic and quartic forms is full-dimensional (in the ambient space of coefficients), for n $\ge$ 2. Also for every odd degree d, the class of benign degree-d forms increases with the dimension (however it does not imply that such forms become more frequent when the dimension increases).

Optimization and Control.title: Control, stability, and stabilization of some classes of linear time-delay systems
Optimization and Control.summary: This monograph presents a selection of the author's recent works on the control, stability, and stabilization of some classes of linear time-delay systems. After a detailed introduction to topics related to time-delay systems covered in the monograph, its main contents are presented in a series of mostly independent chapters.

Optimization and Control.title: Diffusive Stochastic Master Equation (SME) with dispersive qubit/cavity coupling
Optimization and Control.summary: We provide a detailed analysis of the quantum diffusive Stochastic Master Equation~(SME) for qubit/cavity systems with dispersive coupling, incorporating classical input signals and output signals (measurement outcomes via homodyne/heterodyne detection). We show that the dynamics of the qubit/cavity density operator converges exponentially towards a slow invariant manifold. This manifold is parameterized by the density operator of a \emph{fictitious} qubit governed by a quantum SME that incorporates the classical input/output signals while preserving complete positivity and trace. The reduced cavity (resp.\ qubit) operator, obtained by partial trace over the qubit (resp.\ cavity), is then expressed as a time-varying deterministic quantum channel acting on the fictitious-qubit density operator. This formulation avoids the non-Markovian descriptions---with temporarily negative dephasing rates or detection efficiencies exceeding one---that appear in several publications. Extensions are considered in which the qubit is replaced by a qudit dispersively coupled to an arbitrary set of cavity modes driven by collective classical input/output signals.
Optimization and Control.comment: This revised version was prepared with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic)

Optimization and Control.title: Gradient Discrete Schrodinger Bridge Matching for Peptide Generation
Optimization and Control.summary: The optimal control of a discrete Schrödinger bridge is a discrete gradient, a difference of vertex potentials, but recent models such as MadSBM instead learn a free control on the edges by cross-entropy. We prove that this leaves the action uncontrolled: cross-entropy identifies the control only up to a state-dependent shift (a gauge), and the action is $\operatorname{KL}(r\|p)$ plus a gauge term the loss never constrains. We propose GDSBM, which writes the control as a difference of vertex potentials and adds the action to the loss; pinning the gauge costs no expressiveness and makes the action a property of the model, so the penalty acts on the model and not on the gauge. On peptide generation our MadSBM reimplementation has a free-gauge action of order $10^{8}$ for a gauge-fixed value of $6.5$, against $1.5$ for GDSBM, with no quality loss that three seeds can detect. The gradient form also fits guidance, which becomes the addition of a potential: guided toward a net charge of $+3$ at pH~7, GDSBM is closer than MadSBM, over three seeds, to its exact tempered target in total variation at every guidance strength (at $β=1$, $81\%$ of samples in the target window against $74\%$, for a target of $97\%$); we claim no statistical significance.

Optimization and Control.title: Fragility-aware Classification for Risk Characterization and Robust Learning
Optimization and Control.summary: Classification models play a central role in data-driven decision-making applications such as medical diagnosis, recommendation systems, and risk assessment. Traditional performance metrics, such as accuracy and AUC, quantify classification errors and pairwise ranking performance but do not account for the magnitude of errors, i.e., the risk of confident misjudgments. This limitation is particularly consequential in safety-critical and cost-sensitive settings, where overconfident errors can lead to severe outcomes. To address this issue, we propose the Fragility Index (FI), a novel performance metric that evaluates classifiers from a risk-averse perspective by capturing the tail risk of confident misjudgments. We formulate FI within a robust satisficing (RS) framework to quantify classifier sensitivity under distributional uncertainty. Building on this, we develop a tractable surrogate-based training framework and establish provable bounds connecting training fragility to ranking-error FI. We further derive tractable reformulations for a broad class of loss functions, including cross-entropy, hinge-type, and Lipschitz losses, and identify specific conditions under which these reformulations are exact. We also introduce an FI-induced regularizer for deep neural networks. Empirical results on real-world medical diagnosis tasks demonstrate that FI complements existing metrics by revealing error tail risk not reflected in accuracy or AUC. FI-based models achieve competitive predictive performance while generally attaining lower FI. In the simulated human--AI diagnostic workflow, they also achieve lower average operational costs than empirical risk minimization.

Optimization and Control.title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: Approximating the maximum retained energy fraction in globally asymptotically stable quadratic systems of growing dimension is NP-hard at every fixed positive additive error below $1/2$, even when strict quartic Lyapunov functions and strictness proofs are constructed in polynomial time and included in the input. Polynomial-factor approximation is also NP-hard for the least dissipated fraction, energy-halving time and structured coefficient distance to loss of asymptotic stability. For a partially damped family, minimum unit-sphere coupling norm equals that distance, with two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds at distances in $(0,1/2]$ and explicit coefficient factors. Additive hardness persists under structured coefficient perturbations and direct damping, even with global exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian.
Optimization and Control.comment: 7 pages, 3 figures; revised proof exposition and conclusion

Optimization and Control.title: Strong Duality Thresholds and Minimum Curvature for the Nearest Rectangular Symplectic Matrix Problem
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the nearest rectangular symplectic matrix problem in the squared Frobenius norm for arbitrary targets $T\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2k}$, with $n\ge k$. We prove that its semidefinite relaxation is exact for every target if and only if $n\ge2k-1$. Under this condition, the primal problem, the relaxation, and both Lagrangian dual problems attain the same optimal value. In this range, we derive the exact minimum Rayleigh quotient of the Riemannian Hessian at every feasible point under the Euclidean induced metric, and prove that all second-order stationary points are global minimizers. We also obtain global objective error bounds. We extend the strong-duality and minimum-curvature results to Hermitian positive definite row weights, proving that strong duality holds for every target if and only if the lowest eigenvalue of the weight has complex multiplicity at least $2k-1$. The dual formulation leads to a method whose main iterations use matrices of order $2k$, with $O(k^2)$ iterative storage apart from the full input and output. Across six tested sizes, mean-time speedups are $2.55$--$12.60$ over a Riemannian first-order method and $4.61$--$43.93$ over Jensen--Zimmermann R--TR2; batching gives a further factor of $3.45$--$23.53$ over sequential calls. The theoretical results complete the critical dimensions not covered by Gram convexification and quadratic matrix programming.

Optimization and Control.title: Model Predictive Control of Wind Turbines: A Model-Oriented Review of Prediction Models, Control Objectives, and Nonlinear Aerodynamic Formulations
Optimization and Control.summary: Model predictive control (MPC) has been applied to wind-turbine regulation with markedly different internal prediction models, ranging from linearized low-order turbine models to nonlinear, aeroelastic, floating, and data-driven predictors. This review organizes the literature primarily by the model propagated by the controller and treats model order, predictor representation, MPC formulation, control objective, and validation plant as separate descriptors. Primary studies show that low-order linear or piecewise-affine predictors are attractive for constrained power and speed regulation, whereas flexible drivetrain, structural, and floating models are needed when drivetrain twist, tower motion, blade loads, or platform dynamics are explicit control quantities. Nonlinear and economic MPC studies further demonstrate coordinated pitch/torque control across broad operating regions, while preview, repetitive, and data-driven formulations address wind prediction, periodic loads, and model mismatch. Particular attention is given to aerodynamic pitch dependence: variable-pitch turbine dynamics can be non-affine with respect to applied pitch, and the term NMPC alone does not prove that the original nonlinear pitch map is retained inside the optimizer. The review therefore adopts a conservative, equation-based classification for direct nonlinear applied-pitch propagation. Here, direct nonlinear applied-pitch propagation means that the applied pitch at each prediction step is evaluated inside the original nonlinear aerodynamic map, rather than replacing that dependence by a linearized, scheduled, piecewise-affine, or learned surrogate. The literature supports a remaining integration challenge at the intersection of flexible drivetrain prediction, nonlinear aerodynamic pitch treatment, explicit constraints and load objectives, and validated adaptive or learned model correction.
Optimization and Control.comment: Khalili-Amirabadi, R., Jalaeian-Farimani, M., & Ghane, M. (2026). Model Predictive Control of Wind Turbines: A Model-Oriented Review of Prediction Models, Control Objectives, and Nonlinear Aerodynamic Formulations. Journal of Intelligent Monitoring and Control Systems, 1(1): 35-41. https://doi.org/10.65098/jimcs.01.2026.35.41

Optimization and Control.title: Deep ReLU Networks Can Fail the Best Approximation Property for Continuous Target Functions
Optimization and Control.summary: We construct a continuous function on $[-1,1]^2$ for which the infimum of the $L^2$-approximation error over the class of ReLU networks with two hidden layers and architecture $(2,2,1,1)$ is not attained. This counterexample shows that deep ReLU networks do not satisfy the best approximation property in general, even for continuous target functions. Our findings contrast with existing results for shallow neural networks, where ReLU is one of the few activation functions that guarantee the existence of global minima in typical regression tasks. The proof is based on the fact that the breaklines for neurons in the second hidden layer can bend, which breaks the symmetry arguments used in the one-hidden-layer case.

Optimization and Control.title: Exact controllability and rapid stabilization of linear difference delay equations and one-dimensional hyperbolic systems
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper addresses exact controllability and rapid stabilization issues for linear difference delay systems with finitely many pointwise delays. We first establish a criterion for exact controllability in $L^r$, $r \in [1, +\infty)$, characterized by a necessary and sufficient Hautus-type frequency-domain condition. The sufficiency of this condition in $L^r$ was already known [https://hal.science/hal-04830757/], whereas its necessity had previously been established only in $L^1$ [arXiv:2210.13590]. We answer [arXiv:2210.13590, Conjecture 3.8] by proving that this condition is also necessary for $r \in (1, +\infty)$. The analysis is based on rewriting the system as an evolution equation in a suitable Banach space, which allows one to apply duality arguments in the spirit of [https://doi.org/10.1137/S036301299119795X]. Building on this controllability analysis and the abstract stabilization framework developed in [https://doi.org/10.1137/S0363012996301609, arXiv:1301.5744], we prove that our exact controllability criterion in $L^r$ is also a sufficient condition for rapid stabilization in $L^2$, i.e., that the system of interest can be stabilized by a family of state feedback control laws ensuring that the closed-loop system is exponentially stable in $L^2$ with an arbitrarily large decay rate. As an application, we extend our results to linear one-dimensional hyperbolic partial differential equations, which can be reduced to linear difference delay systems via the method of characteristics, obtaining also a necessary and sufficient frequency-domain criterion for exact controllability in $L^r$, $r\in [1, +\infty)$, which, as before, is a sufficient condition for rapid stabilization in $L^2$.

Optimization and Control.title: The Maximal Robust Positively Invariant Set for Linear Difference Inclusions
Optimization and Control.summary: This article develops a systematic characterization and exact computational framework for the maximal robust positively invariant set of linear difference inclusions. The maximal set is characterized as the greatest fixed point of the robust predecessor operator, leading to three equivalent set iterations for its computation. Under uniform exponential stability and bounded disturbances, the Kuratowski upper limit of the disturbance-reachable sets yields a necessary and sufficient condition for the maximal set to be nonempty under closed state constraints. Sufficient conditions for its finite determination are also established, together with an explicit bound on the determination index. For polyhedral state constraints, bounded disturbances, and finite or polytopic matrix families, exact half-space implementations of the three iterations are derived. Although these algorithms generate the same set sequence, complexity analysis and numerical experiments reveal substantial differences in their computational performance.

Optimization and Control.title: Exact value functions and sensitivities for energy storage by fast Legendre transforms
Optimization and Control.summary: Long chains of decisions coupled only through a bounded cumulative state, such as the operation of an energy-storage device, form convex programs that generic solvers treat as arbitrary sparse models. We present an exact solver for this class that propagates the complete convex cost-to-reach function through restrictions and infimal convolutions, each evaluated by fast Legendre-Fenchel conjugation as an ordered merge of slopes: no state grid, no value approximation, and a function rather than a single primal-dual pair as output. Price-taking storage instances of 5,000 to 15,000 hourly steps solve 35-93 times faster than Gurobi. The value function is what pays: exact capacity marginals in one differentiated pass, recourse assembled rather than sampled on scenario trees, and a certified sizing loop whose cut count does not grow with the number of weather years. We then widen the carried state. Two storages at one node can be eliminated rather than coordinated by carrying the value function of the pair, and we prove that this object is combinatorially rigid: every breakline the recursion realizes is vertical, horizontal, or borne by a line through the origin, with no genericity assumption. For d co-located stores sharing one charge-discharge coefficient, every realized wall is a position hyperplane or an indifference hyperplane {s_i = s_j}. A catalogue law maps where speed holds: one-dimensional chains beat the frontal solve by 15-30x and growing, while the planar block loses by 13.5-107x on rich network curves. Those curves are themselves exact, traced by a parametric dual simplex. The open-source package FLToptim, every benchmark driver and all data accompany the paper.
Optimization and Control.comment: 63 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21943668

Optimization and Control.title: An efficient mixed-integer linear programming formulation for solving influence diagrams
Optimization and Control.summary:
Influence diagrams represent decision-making problems with interdependencies between random events, decisions, and consequences. Traditionally, they have been solved using tailored algorithms that determine the expected utility-maximizing decision strategy. Towards this end, most recent state-of-the-art solution approaches convert them into mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models that can be solved using off-the-shelf MILP solvers. Computationally, these approaches are most efficient for influence diagrams that represent periodic (or sequential) decision processes, which can be cast as partially observable Markov Decision Processes. However, they are inefficient for problems that lack this periodic structure or whose influence diagrams have large state spaces.
  The efficient MILP formulation presented in this paper is specifically designed for influence diagrams that are challenging for earlier MILP formulations. Additionally, this formulation can be adapted to optimize conditional value-at-risk and to incorporate chance and logical constraints, thereby retaining the modeling flexibility of MILP-based methods. Finally, computational experiments on a range of problems from the literature are reported to show that the proposed formulation is much more efficient than earlier MILP formulations, particularly in problems which cannot be modeled as partially observable Markov decision processes and which lead to influence diagrams whose decision or chance nodes may have large state spaces.

Optimization and Control.title: Minimality and stability of the ball for the charge-qubit energy
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the shape optimization problem introduced by Mazzoleni, Muratov, and Ruffini as a model for a superconducting charge qubit, in which the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of a set of prescribed volume competes with the Coulomb self-energy of the ground state. We prove that, for sufficiently small charge, the ball is the unique minimizer, and that the energy deficit of a volume-preserving and centered perturbation of the ball is comparable to the squared $H^{1/2}$ norm of the boundary graph, with constants independent of the charge. We also obtain the corresponding results for the quadratic Hartree--Ohta--Kawasaki model.
Optimization and Control.comment: AI tools were used in this project. All mathematical arguments and proofs in the final manuscript were checked and written by the author. A note is added on the independent work of Mazzoleni, Moraschi, and Ruffini (arXiv:2610.29958), which proves ball rigidity for the quadratic model by a second shape derivative argument. No other changes were made

Optimization and Control.title: When Is Two-Stage Sample Robust Optimization Asymptotically Optimal? A Simple Perspective
Optimization and Control.summary: Two-stage sample robust optimization with linear decision rules is a standard data-driven approach to two-stage stochastic linear programs with unknown distributions. \cite{bertsimas2022two} established that this approach is asymptotically optimal under several conditions. Most conditions are mild, but one imposes a technical requirement on the recourse system. Whether this condition is implied by the others was left as an open question. We resolve this open question through a geometric feature of the support set: simpleness, the property that every vertex is incident to exactly as many edges as the dimension of the support. For simple support sets, the technical condition is automatic, and asymptotic optimality holds under the remaining standard assumptions. For every non-simple support, we construct a recourse system that is feasible everywhere in the support but violates the technical condition, and this construction resolves the open question. We further characterize the simpleness of one-sided and two-sided budgeted uncertainty sets and identify when budget perturbations can restore simpleness. We also develop a polynomial-time algorithm that certifies the technical condition at a given vertex using its incident edge directions. Numerical experiments on newsvendor and network lot-sizing problems illustrate the characterization and the effectiveness of the verification algorithm.

Optimization and Control.title: On Modified Newton Methods for Unconstrained Optimization Based on Lanczos Tridiagonalization
Optimization and Control.summary: For a strongly convex unconstrained minimization problem, Newton's method with a line search offers rapid convergence to a minimizer by incorporating second-order information. However, for a general unconstrained problem the Hessian need not be positive definite, which can lead to the inability to find a search direction or to search directions that fail to produce descent. Modified Newton methods are designed to handle this situation. This paper considers modifications to a Newton-conjugate-gradient approach based on Lanczos tridiagonalization. Existing methods are extended using dynamic modification schemes that provide a descent direction while keeping the modification bounded. A Lanczos-based scheme and a conjugate-gradient (CG)-based scheme are formulated and analyzed. These methods are mathematically equivalent in exact arithmetic, but their practical behavior differs in finite precision. Finally, it is shown how the convergence and computational cost are affected by varying the amount of additional curvature introduced and by allowing the early termination of the inner iterations.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Network Dependence in Distributed Stochastic Optimization via Tree Routing
Optimization and Control.summary: Communication is a central bottleneck in distributed optimization, but its effect is often summarized by the spectral gap of a chosen mixing matrix. Since this gap depends on link weights as well as topology, it can obscure the intrinsic effect of the network. We clarify this distinction by relating graph diameter to the inverse spectral gap. We establish a universal one-sided bound that is tight up to constant factors, while constructions across several graph families show that no topology-only converse or universal two-sided scaling law exists. This motivates a class-based view of network optimality: diameter-dependent guarantees can be assessed uniformly over graph classes, whereas spectral-gap optimality requires both the graph--matrix pair class and the admissible algorithm class to be specified. Based on the resulting diameter-based minimax benchmark, we introduce Tree-Routed Gradient Tracking (Tree-RGT), a distributed method for stochastic nonconvex optimization. The method pipelines model dissemination and gradient aggregation over a rooted shortest-path spanning tree. Each iteration uses one round of one-hop communication and one stochastic-gradient evaluation per agent, without inner consensus or multi-gossip. Under smoothness and unbiased bounded-variance oracles, Tree-RGT achieves uniformly optimal network dependence over connected graphs of prescribed size and diameter. It recovers centralized stochastic scaling after $\mathcal{O}(nD_{\mathcal{G}}^2)$ transient iterations, where $n$ is the number of agents and $D_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the graph diameter. This network-dependent transient-iteration bound improves upon or matches those reported for representative distributed methods. Thus, topology-aware routing attains diameter-optimal guarantees without relying on a prescribed mixing matrix.

Optimization and Control.title: Policy Evaluation and Policy Gradient for Continuous-Time Markov Regime-Switching Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: We study policy evaluation (PE) and policy gradient (PG) for continuous-time stochastic control with Markov regime-switching. The main challenges are the coexistence of diffusion and regime jumps, the coupling of regime-dependent value functions, and the construction of model-free learning rules from the coupled generators. We establish a martingale characterization of PE that incorporates both Brownian and switching martingales, and extend martingale loss and orthogonality methods to this setting. We further derive a coupled PG equation and a trajectory-based gradient representation that, under an action-independent switching generator, avoids explicit knowledge of the system coefficients and transition rates. These results lead to offline and online actor-critic algorithms. We also establish convergence and study the finite-grid approximation required for implementation. Numerical experiments for a regime-switching linear-quadratic problem illustrate the proposed methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Safety-constrained position tracking of a flexible transmission system
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider safety-constrained position tracking for a flexible transmission system consisting of a torsional shaft driven by a motor and connected to a gravitationally loaded inertia. The coupled PDE-ODE dynamics admit a semilinear formulation in which the linear input-output system is impedance passive and the gravitational torque enters as a bounded, globally Lipschitz perturbation. We establish an energy dissipation inequality for the nonlinear model and show that a position-funnel controller with supervised damping admits a unique global closed-loop trajectory. In particular, the motor-angle tracking error remains strictly inside a prescribed time-varying funnel, which can be chosen to enforce safety bounds on the motor angle.

Optimization and Control.title: ItsDEAL: Inexact two-level smoothing descent algorithms for weakly convex optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper addresses nonconvex optimization problems via a two-level smoothing framework, where the high-order Moreau envelope (HOME) provides a smooth approximation of weakly convex cost functions. We study the differentiability and weak smoothness of HOME. Building on the inexact two-level smoothing optimization framework (ItsOPT), we propose an inexact two-level smoothing descent algorithm (ItsDEAL) by: (i) approximately solving the proximal subproblem to obtain an inexact first-order oracle for HOME at the lower level; and (ii) applying an inexact first-order method at the upper level. We derive computable sufficient conditions for lower-level inexactness, enabling approximate high-order proximal-points to be certified without access to the exact proximal-point or HOME value. In particular, we study a parameter-free Hölderian inexact gradient method and an inexact descent method with Armijo line search, both exploiting the weak smoothness of HOME. We establish subsequential convergence under mild inexactness assumptions, and global and linear convergence under the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz (KL) property. Preliminary experiments on ridge-regularized hinge-loss classification, a high-dimensional MCP-regularized classification model, and robust matrix completion illustrate the numerical behavior of the proposed methods and the role of the HOME order.

Optimization and Control.title: Assortment optimization under the perception-adjusted Luce model
Optimization and Control.summary: The Perception-Adjusted Luce Model (PALM) introduced by by Echenique et al. (2018) is a sequential choice model that can accommodate violations of regularity and choice overload, behaviors not captured by the utility-maximization framework. Flores et al. (2019) studied the assortment problem under the PALM and proved that, for the case of two levels, there is always an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level. They also conjectured that revenue-ordered by levels remain optimal for the general PALM with any number of levels. We resolve this question in the affirmative by showing that every PALM instance admits an optimal assortment that includes, within each level, all products at or above a level-specific revenue threshold. The proof involves first showing how the conjecture which deals with a discrete optimization problem, can be reduced to proving certain property of a related continuous optimization problem. Specifically, we study a continuous refinement of the assortment decision under the same PALM choice rule. Although the refinement permits partial utility selections, we prove it always has an optimum that selects complete revenue tiers. This allows us to show that the assortment problem is polynomial-time solvable when the number of levels is fixed.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Deterministic First-Order Oracle Complexity for Nonconvex-Concave Minimax Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the deterministic first-order oracle complexity of smooth nonconvex-concave minimax optimization over a bounded convex dual domain under two notions of stationarity: optimization stationarity (OS) and game stationarity (GS). OS concerns stationarity of the value function, viewed as a structured nonsmooth objective obtained by maximizing over the dual variable. GS concerns the joint first-order optimality conditions for both primal minimization and dual maximization, each with the other variable held fixed. Existing upper bounds on the oracle complexity of first-order methods for finding $ε$-OS and $ε$-GS points have different dependence on $ε$, but whether this difference reflects an intrinsic separation in computational hardness remains unresolved. We resolve this question by establishing worst-case lower bounds for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods: $Ω(ε^{-3})$ oracle queries for finding an $ε$-OS point and $Ω(ε^{-5/2})$ for finding an $ε$-GS point, with the remaining problem parameters fixed. These bounds match existing upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. To close the remaining logarithmic gap, we introduce Tracked-FOAM, a new first-order algorithm whose oracle complexity matches our lower bounds for both OS and GS. Together, these results establish an intrinsic separation between OS and GS in the optimal accuracy dependence of deterministic first-order oracle complexity.
Optimization and Control.comment: v2: Established matching bounds for both OS and GS across all parameter regimes, revealing an intrinsic separation in optimal accuracy dependence

Optimization and Control.title: Sum of Squares and Non Sum of Squares Regimes for the Toeplitz Bottcher Wenzel Form
Optimization and Control.summary: Toeplitz matrices are among the simplest structured models of translation invariance, arising naturally in convolution, stationary covariance models, and discretizations of translation-invariant operators. For a pair of real matrices, the Böttcher--Wenzel form (BW form) is a nonnegative quartic measuring the gap in the corresponding commutator inequality. László conjectured that, when both matrices are Toeplitz, this quartic is a sum of squares for every matrix order. We show that the conjecture is false. More precisely, we identify an explicit family of corner-supported Toeplitz pairs, retaining only the outermost diagonals on the two sides, for which the associated BW form is not a sum of squares at all sufficiently large orders. The proof reduces the complete family of Gram representations to a finite complex test: its Gram-invariant part develops a strictly negative limiting direction, while the remaining Gram-dependent contribution vanishes. We also give an explicit sufficient threshold for the matrix order. The negative result is complemented by two positive regimes. If either Toeplitz factor is symmetric or skew-symmetric, then the corresponding BW form is SoS for every order, with the other factor allowed to be an arbitrary real Toeplitz matrix. For unrestricted Toeplitz pairs, we further prove SoS representability for every $2\le N\le50$, with formal Lean~4 verification through order 20. The large-order non-SoS theorem, including the explicit sufficient threshold, has also been formally verified in Lean 4.

Optimization and Control.title: LLM-Guided Transportation Hub Capacity Planning with Textual Business Inputs
Optimization and Control.summary: While traditional hub capacity planning models optimize effectively for quantitative inputs, they often fail to digest qualitative business context. We propose a novel framework where a large language model (LLM) agent iteratively proposes hub capacity decisions guided by natural-language business context descriptions. The key mechanism is a chain-of-thought reasoning protocol: the LLM constructs a structured decision table that maps each contextual item to specific capacity adjustments based on the implied direction and magnitude of changes. The new capacity decision is then validated through a feedback loop with an optimization model, which provides routing-based performance metrics to guide the agent's selection. On a real-world 13-hub freight network in the southeastern US, our framework achieves a 2.8% optimality gap relative to the hidden ground-truth, a significant improvement over the 11.0% gap produced by the traditional optimization model without textual business inputs. This demonstrates that LLMs can serve as a contextual bridge, integrating qualitative business insights into Operations Research workflows.

Optimization and Control.title: Analysis of On-policy Policy Gradient Methods under the Distribution Mismatch
Optimization and Control.summary: Policy gradient methods are among the most successful approaches for solving challenging reinforcement learning problems. Despite their empirical success, many state-of-the-art policy gradient algorithms for discounted problems estimate update directions using a sampling distribution that differs from the discounted state distribution required by the policy gradient theorem. In this work, we analyze the impact of this distribution mismatch on policy gradient methods. Specifically, {for tabular direct and softmax parameterizations, we establish global convergence of objective values under biased updates}. {For tabular softmax policies, we further derive the exact leading-order coefficients of the asymptotic objective errors under biased and normalized exact updates. Their ratio provides an explicit criterion for determining when distribution mismatch accelerates or slows asymptotic convergence.} We then extend the analysis to more general policy parameterizations by deriving explicit bounds on both the state distribution mismatch and the induced normalized policy-gradient mismatch in episodic and continuing MDPs. These mismatches vanish at least linearly as the discount factor approaches one. Under an additional smoothness assumption, we further show that the limit inferior of the squared norm of the normalized exact policy-gradient direction along the biased iterates is bounded by $O((1-γ)^2)$ in both settings. Our results provide theoretical insights into the robustness of policy gradient methods to distribution mismatch and shed light on the gap between their theoretical formulations and practical implementations.

Optimization and Control.title: Hidden Convexity of the Joint Range of Three Quadratic Forms and Applications
Optimization and Control.summary:
We investigate a hidden convexity phenomenon for triples of homogeneous
  quadratic forms. We give a complete characterization of the convexity of
  the upper image obtained by adding the nonnegative orthant to their joint
  range. More precisely, the upper image is convex if and only if either a
  nonzero nonnegative linear combination of the three associated matrices is
  positive semidefinite, or the three quadratic forms admit a common strict
  negative direction. In particular, the upper image is convex whenever one
  of the three quadratic forms is convex. As applications, we establish the
  convexity of an associated value function and derive a generalized S-lemma
  for implications involving two quadratic inequalities and a strict theorem
  of the alternative for quadratic systems.

Optimization and Control.title: Adaptive Restart under Unknown KL Geometry in Stochastic Weakly-Convex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: KL geometry accelerates restart schedules in stochastic weakly-convex optimization, but the schedule depends jointly on an unknown and potentially nonunique geometric description. We introduce CARP-KL, a certified portfolio that adapts over valid KL descriptions while using the same primitive stochastic-subgradient oracle for both optimization and candidate selection. Over declared polynomial parameter ranges, CARP-KL competes with every affordable valid description and preserves the known-description polynomial Moreau-stationarity rate up to logarithmic factors, without objective values, an exact proximal map, direct Moreau-gradient access, or a bounded-domain assumption. Controlled experiments quantify the finite-budget price of this universality. The portfolio repeatedly contains strong candidates, while certification consumes a substantial share of the oracle budget and finite-sample ranking limits their recovery. A common conservative gap bound further reduces the portfolio from $O(\log^3 T)$ to $O(\log^2 T)$ candidates with an explicit scale-mismatch penalty. The theory and diagnostics together establish certified unknown-geometry adaptation and pinpoint selection as the principal practical frontier of the current construction.

Optimization and Control.title: Sinkhorn Distributionally Robust State Estimation via System Level Synthesis
Optimization and Control.summary: In state estimation tasks, the usual assumption of an exactly known disturbance distribution is often unrealistic and renders the estimator fragile in practice. The recently emerging Wasserstein distributionally robust state estimation (DRSE) design can partially mitigate this fragility; however, its worst-case distribution is provably discrete, which deviates from the inherent continuity of real-world distributions and results in over-pessimism. In this work, we develop a new Sinkhorn DRSE design within the system level synthesis scheme with the aim of shaping the closed-loop errors under the unknown continuous disturbance distribution. For uncertainty description, we adopt the Sinkhorn ambiguity set that includes an entropic regularizer to penalize non-smooth and discrete distributions within a Wasserstein ball. We present the first result of finite-sample probabilistic guarantee of the Sinkhorn ambiguity set. Then we analyze the limiting properties of our Sinkhorn DRSE design, thereby highlighting its close connection with the generic $\mathcal{H}_2$ design and Wasserstein DRSE. To tackle the min-max optimization problem, we reformulate it as a finite-dimensional convex program through duality theory. By identifying a compact subset of the feasible set guaranteed to enclose the global optimum, we develop a tailored Frank-Wolfe solution algorithm and formally establish its convergence rate. The advantage of Sinkhorn DRSE over existing design schemes is verified through numerical case studies.

Optimization and Control.title: Retraction-Free Nonsmooth Optimization on the Stiefel Manifold: Subgradient and Proximal Landing Methods
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop three retraction-free Landing methods for nonsmooth composite optimization over the Stiefel manifold, combining an (approximately) tangential direction with an infeasibility-reducing normal direction. The subgradient Landing method, with normal stepsizes parameterized by $α\in[0,1]$, has best-iterate complexity bounds $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ for surrogate stationarity and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2/(2-α)})$ for feasibility. For $α=0$, it converges locally $R$-linearly under local weak sharpness and mild assumptions. The proximal gradient Landing method computes a tangential direction by solving a proximal subproblem and combines it with the same normal direction. Moreover, the inexact proximal gradient Landing method allows the proximal subproblem to be solved approximately and applies an explicit correction to control violations of the tangency condition. Both proximal methods have outer-iteration complexity bounds $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ for stationarity and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-1})$ for feasibility, and every accumulation point is first-order stationary. Under an additional asymptotic Bregman-error condition and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property of a suitable auxiliary function, the primal sequence of the inexact method converges to a first-order stationary point. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of all three methods. On the tested sparse principal component analysis instances, the inexact method has favorable running times, and both proximal methods maintain small feasibility residuals.

Optimization and Control.title: Opinion dynamics on switching networks
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study opinion dynamics over a two-layer multiplex network with weighted, directed influence and reciprocal links. Within each layer, an agent weighs its neighbors equally, so the influence of a neighbor is inversely proportional to the agent's number of neighbors in that layer. Agents update their opinions over time to coordinate with their neighbors. However, the frequency of agents' interactions with neighbors in different network layers differs: one layer is always active, whereas the other one is active only once every $k$ time steps.
  Consequently, the multiplex network's adjacency matrices are time-varying.
  We characterize how the activation frequency of the second layer impacts the convergence of the opinion dynamics process. Without requiring agents to place positive weight on their own opinions, we prove that, for every activation period $k$, the opinions reach a consensus whose value depends on $k$, and that the asymptotic per-step convergence factor equals the $k$th root of the second-largest eigenvalue modulus of the one-period transition matrix. As $k$ grows, this factor generically converges to that of the always-active layer when this layer is connected; when it is disconnected, the time to consensus generically grows linearly in $k$. Numerical experiments on 1,000 random multiplex networks confirm these results.

Optimization and Control.title: Soft-Update MSA for Nonconvex Stochastic Optimal Control: Theory and Algorithms
Optimization and Control.summary: For the method of successive approximations (MSA), a fundamental challenge is that the stochastic maximum principle (SMP) provides an optimality condition rather than a descent rule. To overcome this difficulty for nonconvex stochastic control problems, we develop a soft-update MSA (SU-MSA) with a second-order-adjoint correction of the Hamiltonian and a neural realization called DeepSMP. Both an explicit stepsize rule guaranteeing cost descent and the convergence of the algorithm are established. Moreover, the global SMP condition is asymptotically satisfied when the corrected Hamiltonian is convex, while in a special case the cost is further proved to converge to the global optimum. To extend SU-MSA to high dimensions, we develop DeepSMP using a differentiable smooth approximation of the corrected Hamiltonian and analyze the convergence of the resulting objective and its gradient. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Two-Mode Switching with Setup Costs for a Controlled Ornstein--Uhlenbeck Process
Optimization and Control.summary: We study an infinite-horizon discounted optimal switching problem for an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process whose mean-reversion level can be switched between two values. Switching incurs positive, potentially asymmetric fixed costs, and the mode with the higher mean-reversion level entails an additional running cost. The revenue rate is proportional to the positive part of the state. We characterize the value function and identify parameter conditions under which an optimal policy either remains permanently in one mode after a possible costly initial switch or follows a threshold rule. The threshold formulation allows infinite boundaries and therefore includes one-way switching. A key technical contribution is to establish existence and uniqueness of the relevant solutions to the coupled nonlinear free-boundary equations arising from value-matching and smooth-fit conditions. In the corresponding parameter regimes, these solutions determine the finite switching thresholds and the coefficients of the candidate value functions. A verification argument then establishes the optimality of the resulting policies over all admissible switching strategies.

Optimization and Control.title: OFF Newton-type Methods for Unconstrained Optimization with Inexact Derivatives
Optimization and Control.summary: We study objective-function-free (OFF) Newton-type methods for smooth unconstrained optimization with inexact gradients and Hessians. We propose two methods for first- and second-order stationarity, coupling explicit step-size rules with derivative-accuracy and linear-solver residual conditions to guarantee sufficient decrease without evaluating the objective function. The OFF regularized Newton method finds an $\varepsilon$-first-order stationary point in $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations. Under strong convexity, a local Newton variant converges with \(Q\)-order at least $1+θ$, where \(θ\in (0, 1]\). For second-order stationarity, we combine regularized Newton steps with approximate eigenvectors associated with the minimum eigenvalue. With high probability, the resulting method finds an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{L_h\varepsilon})$-second-order stationary point in $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3/2})$ iterations, using a total of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-7/4})$ approximate gradient evaluations and Hessian-vector products. For finite-sum problems, we develop subsampling schemes that yield best-iterate convergence in expectation in the nonconvex first-order setting and local \(R\)-linear convergence with high probability in the strongly convex setting, followed by \(Q\)-order at least \(1+θ\) once full sampling is reached. The subsampled second-order method achieves a high-probability $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-7/2})$ total sample-operation bound, counting component gradient evaluations and component Hessian-vector products.

Robotics.title: Motion Retargeting with Spatiotemporal Preferences for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.

Robotics.title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
Robotics.summary: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.

Robotics.title: Principles of Robot Autonomy
Robotics.summary: Autonomous robots are moving rapidly from research labs into everyday life - on roads, in the air, in warehouses, and in space. Robot autonomy is no longer solely an academic pursuit, but a collection of mature, field-tested methods and tools that practitioners rely on in real-world deployments. This book offers a clear, unified introduction to the methods that make this possible. Built on decades of teaching at Stanford, the text develops the core elements of modern autonomy stacks within a single conceptual framework, bridging classical robotics and modern physical AI. Every major topic is paired with hands-on Jupyter notebooks and implementation-driven exercises, so readers build practical intuition alongside theoretical understanding. The result is a principled, accessible, and deployment-aware foundation for anyone seeking to design, analyze, or contribute to the next generation of autonomous systems. This is a comprehensive resource for students, engineers, and researchers entering one of today's fastest-growing fields.
Robotics.comment: 531 pages. Pre-publication version of a book forthcoming from Cambridge University Press, posted with the permission of the publisher

Robotics.title: PhysibleMDM: Enforcing Inference-Time Physical Feasibility Constraints on Motion Diffusion Models via Noise Optimization
Robotics.summary: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.

Robotics.title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
Robotics.summary: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
Robotics.comment: 28 pages. A 5-page version appears at the CL4FMAgents workshop, NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). Code and pre-registration: https://github.com/TPEmist/AionGenos

Robotics.title: UniMem: Unifying Visual and Textual Memory in VLAs for Non-Markovian Tasks
Robotics.summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged internet-scale pretraining and task-specific finetuning to achieve strong performance on long-horizon tasks, they often struggle with non-Markovian tasks that require memory. Existing approaches to memory typically involve additional Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) for long-term memory management, introducing a memory bottleneck and a fractured training pipeline. Conditioning on multiple historical frames can provide the VLA with access to more descriptive features of past scenes, but can degrade performance if frames are chosen at arbitrary, fixed intervals. To address these limitations, we present UniMem, a framework that unifies high-level visual and textual memory and low-level control under one backbone. UniMem employs an event classifier to initiate textual and visual memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense visual memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize overhead during policy rollouts. We evaluate UniMem across five simulation and four hardware tasks targeting sequential and spatial memory, demonstrating that our unified, single-model system outperforms fixed-interval image sampling baselines (93.4% vs. 68.2%) in simulation and hierarchical VLM-VLA baselines (80.0% vs. 43.5%) in hardware, while offering faster inference and a simple training pipeline for easy adoption. Project website: https://losterberg3.github.io/unimem-vla/

Robotics.title: Integrated Respiratory Sensing and Gated Control for Autonomous Needle Insertion Via CT Bore Robotic Arm
Robotics.summary: Currently, CT-guided lung biopsy is a highly manual procedure requiring patient breath-holding, iterative manual needle insertions, and repeated CT confirmation scans to accurately target a tumor. Automating this process within the CT bore--without relying on manual needle placement or patient breath-holding--has the potential to reduce procedure time, patient discomfort, and radiation exposure. In this work, we present an integrated sensing and control system capable of performing a gated needle insertion within the CT bore. The experiments demonstrate the system's ability to track and predict patient breath cycles, perform autonomous respiratory-gated needle insertion, and detect breath cycle anomalies.

Robotics.title: The Bitter Lesson Comes to Robotics
Robotics.summary: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate nine models at multiple reasoning-effort and service-tier settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget. However, these capabilities are improving rapidly: performance increases on our benchmark between July and October 2026 (inclusive) correspond to a performance doubling time of 53.9 days, while the best recorded execution rate increased by a factor of 4.4 and the lowest recorded execution cost fell by a factor of 6.2. These trends raise the possibility that the Bitter Lesson is coming to robotics; the capabilities of embodied general purpose LMs may one day be comparable to those of more specialized models.
Robotics.comment: Submitted to the Workshop on The Action Gap (TAG) at CoRL 2026, updated with Gemini Flash 3.6 and Gemini 4 Argon

Robotics.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
Robotics.summary: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
Robotics.comment: 30 pages. Author accepted manuscript. Posted with permission from the Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10; copyright 2027 the author(s), https://www.annualreviews.org. Published version: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-control-032125-030330

Robotics.title: Integrated Longitudinal and Lateral Control for High-Speed Platooning of Articulated Vehicles
Robotics.summary: This paper presents an integrated control framework for high-speed platooning of articulated vehicles, combining advanced longitudinal and lateral control strategies to address the challenges of safe and efficient autonomous driving. A novel proof of string stability for the proposed longitudinal control algorithm, based on a PID framework, ensures robust inter-vehicle distance regulation even under dynamic operating conditions. Additionally, an arc-length-based longitudinal error formulation enhances the applicability of the control system for curved roads, making it realistic for diverse driving scenarios. For lateral control, significant improvements to the clothoid-based path tracking algorithm are introduced to mitigate oscillations and enhance stability at high speeds. These enhancements include a tangential criterion for oscillation reduction, trajectory segment classification for adaptive lookahead distance tuning, a dual-adaptive mechanism for regulating the rate of lookahead distance adjustments based on both cross-track error (CTE) and anticipated road curvature, and extensions for articulated vehicle dynamics. The proposed integrated control framework is validated through simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining stability, minimizing tracking errors, and ensuring robust performance in high-speed and challenging platooning scenarios.
Robotics.comment: Original manuscript of an article published in Vehicle System Dynamics on September 20, 2026. Published version: https://doi.org/10.1080/00423114.2026.2733699

Robotics.title: What Does It Take For A Generalist Robot Policy To Adapt Using Minimal Data?
Robotics.summary: A central goal in robot learning is to move beyond task-specific human data collection toward robots that improve through autonomous interaction. Yet fully autonomous learning remains difficult with current policies: sparse rewards and weak zero-shot exploration often prevent online learning from discovering successful behavior. As a first step towards fully autonomous learning, we propose the minimal-data adaptation regime, in which a pretrained robot policy must learn a new task from as little as one demonstration followed by autonomous online interaction. We establish that, although pretrained policies fail zero-shot on many new tasks, a single demonstration suffices to direct their behavioral prior to coarse task-following behavior, albeit with unreliable performance. From this insight, we isolate the key design principles required to convert coarse task-following into reliable task success. These include (1) the surprising efficacy of pretrained VLA representations to support sample-efficient value learning from online interaction (2) the sufficiency of residual policy learning to learn corrective behavior and (3) the need for careful data-balancing to prevent exploration collapse. As a representative of these principles, we propose MiDAS, a simple offline-to-online RL recipe that combines few-demonstration behavior cloning with value-based residual learning over frozen VLA representations. Across LIBERO and RoboCasa tasks, MiDAS substantially improves performance from single-demonstration initializations, including policies that succeed only rarely, validating the principles highlighted above. On a bimanual YAM platform, starting from a brittle initial policy, MiDAS improves task success after approximately six hours of online interaction.

Robotics.title: Multilaminate piezoelectric polymer actuators for insect-scale softrobots
Robotics.summary: Piezoelectric ceramics enable fast, precise, and powerful actuation with integrated sensing in insect-scale robots. However, they are brittle, failing at low strains limiting its applications involving high impacts, unexpected loading, or soft robotics. To address this limitation, we investigate polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) as a compliant alternative: it tolerates substantially larger strains, but its low piezoelectric coefficient limits the output of conventional single-layer actuators. We demonstrate a novel manufacturing process for multilayer PVDF actuators that utilizes off the shelf materials and provides parallel bussing of signal voltage to reduce integration complexity. Using first principles models validated with experiments, we show a tradeoff between force (linear or superlinear increase with layer count) and displacement (cubic decrease with layer count) for the actuator geometry chosen. Our work positions PVDF actuation an optimization problem for future robotic applications with clear design knobs available to meet performance demands. Further, we show that using thinner PVDF layers within a stack increases the specific power density of the actuators making them ideal for size, weight, and power (SWAP) limitations in small scale robotics. Among the actuators fabricated, >9 mm of free deflection, >20 mN of blocked force, and >500 Hz bandwidth were achieved. To illustrate their potential in future robust robotic platforms, we integrate our actuators into a low-profile insect-scale robot that leverages resonance to achieve planar locomotion while being robust to large external impacts.

Robotics.title: Soft Robotic Exogloves for Dexterous Mobility -- Towards Personalized Rehabilitation
Robotics.summary: Soft robotic exogloves can provide hand rehabilitation and assistance. Fitting these gloves often relies on standardized measurements not tailored to the individual, limiting their effectiveness, especially for fine articulation necessary for dexterous manipulation. We present the design, fabrication, modeling, and testing of a personalized pneumatically-actuated soft robotic exoglove. The glove was fit to a user's hand with topological scans and fabricated with silicone mold casting. Finite element analysis (FEA) was performed to evaluate actuator bending and forces from physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) between an actuator and a simplified personalized biomechanical finger model. Pneumatic pressure control experiments were conducted to flex the user's finger with static and dynamic references. Fabrication results show that topological scans enable precise tailoring to hand anatomy. Simulations showed that anatomical personalization enables analysis of pHRI contact forces, and results indicate sufficient joint mobilization with non-ideal compression on the proximal phalanx. Pneumatic testing indicates that pressure control allows accurate and targeted mobility of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints with intrinsic stiffness. Testing of multiple designs showed that relaxing the strain-limiting layer improves actuator-to-finger joint alignment during actuation. This work presents personalization to the human hand in structural conformability, joint topology, modeling of pHRI contact, and time-dependent actuation-deformation profiles. This lays the groundwork for informing exoglove design optimization to enable assistance in dexterous manipulation and neuromuscular rehabilitation of fine motor skills.
Robotics.comment: 8 pages, 14 figures. Accepted in IEEE Transactions on Medical Robotics and Bionics (T-MRB) 2026

Robotics.title: MPBRS: Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Unified Reward Configuration in Humanoid Locomotion
Robotics.summary: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.

Robotics.title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
Robotics.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models.
